questions.prompt: With \(B\) symmetric positive definite, the set of points \(B u + d\) for \(\lVert u\rVert \le 1\) is
options: the unit disk, for every \(B\) and every center \(d\)
a polygon, because \(B\) is a matrix
a half-space whose boundary passes through \(d\)
an ellipsoid centered at \(d\), with its shape fixed by \(B\)
questions.explanation: \(B\) maps the unit disk to an elliptical disk, and adding \(d\) moves the center. Different positive definite matrices give different shapes, so the set is not always the unit disk. A matrix image of a disk is not a polygon. A half-space is unbounded, and this set is the image of a bounded disk.

questions.prompt: Take \(B = \mathrm{diag}(2,\ 1)\), normal \(a = (3,\ 0)\), and center \(d = (1,\ 4)\). What is \(\lVert B a\rVert + a^T d\)?
questions.explanation: \(B a = (6,\ 0)\), so the length is \(6\). The center term is \(3 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 4 = 3\). The sum is \(9\). Reporting \(6\) drops the center term. Reporting \(3\) drops the length. Reporting \(10\) would be a half-space bound, and no bound was given. The containment test compares this sum with the bound. It does not square the length.

questions.prompt: Maximizing \(\log\det B\) over the containment inequalities is a convex problem because
options: the unit disk \(\lVert u\rVert \le 1\) is the decision variable
every ellipsoid has the same volume, so the objective does not matter
\(\log\det\) is concave on positive definite matrices, and each containment inequality cuts a convex set
\(\log\det\) is a linear function of the entries of \(B\)
questions.explanation: A concave objective, maximized over a convex feasible set, is a convex problem. Equivalently one minimizes \(-\log\det B\), which is convex. The logarithm of the determinant is not linear in the entries. The decision variables are the center and the shape, not a point \(u\) inside the ellipsoid. Different shapes have different determinants, so the volume is the objective.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that checks one half-space \(a^T x \le \beta\) against one ellipsoid. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The length is the length of \(B a\), so the product comes first. The center term is added to that length, so the length comes before the sum. The keep-or-reject step compares the sum with the bound, so it comes last. Comparing with \(\beta\) before the sum exists, or taking a length before \(B a\) exists, is not a reordering of these steps.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded half-plane</title><line x1="36" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><polygon points="70,150 210,40 250,40 250,170 70,170" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.15"/><line x1="60" y1="158" x2="220" y2="30" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A straight boundary with one side shaded.
steps: Multiply the shape matrix \(B\) by the outward normal \(a\).
Take the Euclidean length of the vector that multiplication produced.
Add the center term \(a^T d\) to that length.
Keep the half-space only when the sum just obtained is at most the bound \(\beta\).

questions.prompt: The closed strip \(-2 \le x_1 \le 2\) is the pair of inequalities \(x_1 \le 2\) and \(-x_1 \le 2\). Which ellipsoids \(\{B u + d : \lVert u\rVert \le 1\}\) lie in the strip? \(B\) is diagonal with positive diagonal entries.
questions.explanation:
For \(B = \mathrm{diag}(p,\ q)\) with \(p > 0\), the two inequalities reduce to \(p + d_1 \le 2\) and \(p - d_1 \le 2\). The second diagonal entry and the second coordinate of the center do not appear.
• \(\mathrm{diag}(1,\ 1)\) at the origin gives \(1 \le 2\) on both sides.
• \(\mathrm{diag}(0.5,\ 3)\) with \(d_1 = 1\) gives \(1.5 \le 2\) and \(-0.5 \le 2\).
• \(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ 0.5)\) at the origin meets the bound with equality, which the closed strip allows.
• A center at \((0,\ 5)\) still has \(d_1 = 0\), so the strip, which does not see \(x_2\), still holds.
• \(\mathrm{diag}(1,\ 1)\) with \(d_1 = 1.5\) gives \(2.5 > 2\) on the right-hand face.

questions.prompt: \(B = \mathrm{diag}(p,\ q)\) with \(p\) and \(q\) positive, the normal is \((1,\ 0)\), and the center is \((c,\ 0)\). The containment left-hand side \(\lVert B a\rVert + a^T d\) equals
questions.explanation: \(B a = (p,\ 0)\), and \(p\) is positive, so the length is \(p\). The center term is \(c\). The sum is \(p + c\). The second diagonal entry is multiplied by the zero component of the normal, so \(q\) does not appear. Reporting \(p\) drops the center. Reporting \(q + c\) uses the diagonal entry the normal does not see. Both declared names appear.

questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.

questions.prompt: A note checks the unit disk, \(B = I\) and \(d = 0\), against the half-space \(x_1 + x_2 \le 1\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: \(B\) is the identity, so \(B a = a = (1,\ 1)\). The length \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}\) is \(\sqrt{2}\). The center is the origin, so the center term is \(0\). The containment sum is \(\sqrt{2}\), and \(\sqrt{2} > 1\), so the inequality fails. The unit disk sticks out through the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\). The false step is the comparison of \(\sqrt{2}\) with \(1\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded half-plane</title><line x1="36" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><polygon points="70,150 210,40 250,40 250,170 70,170" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.15"/><line x1="60" y1="158" x2="220" y2="30" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A straight boundary with one side shaded.
steps: Since \(\sqrt{2} \le 1\), the unit disk lies in the half-space.
reasons: \(\sqrt{2}\) is greater than \(1\), so the unit disk is not inside the half-space.
The center term \(a^T d\) is not \(0\).

questions.prompt: Take \(B = \mathrm{diag}(3,\ 1)\), normal \(a = (0,\ 4)\), and center \(d = (2,\ 1)\). What is \(\lVert B a\rVert + a^T d\)?
questions.explanation: \(B a = (0,\ 4)\), so the length is \(4\). The center term is \(0 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 1 = 4\). The sum is \(8\). Reporting \(4\) keeps only one of the two equal terms. Reporting \(16\) squares the length instead of using it. Reporting \(3\) is the unused diagonal entry. The first column of \(B\) is invisible to this normal.

questions.prompt: \(\log\det\) of \(\mathrm{diag}(4,\ 1)\) and of \(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ 2)\) compare as follows.
options: Neither is defined, because a diagonal matrix is not positive definite
They are equal, because both determinants equal \(4\)
\(\mathrm{diag}(4,\ 1)\) is larger, because of the entry \(4\)
\(\mathrm{diag}(2,\ 2)\) is larger, because a rounder shape always has larger determinant
questions.explanation: The determinant of a positive diagonal matrix is the product of the diagonal entries. Both products equal \(4\), so the logarithms agree and the two ellipsoids have the same volume factor. A single large entry does not raise the determinant if another entry shrinks to compensate. Roundness is not the definition of the determinant. Both matrices have positive diagonal entries, so both are positive definite.

questions.prompt: If \(B\) is symmetric positive semidefinite and singular, the set \(\{B u + d : \lVert u\rVert \le 1\}\) is
options: a flat elliptical disk, with volume zero
a full-dimensional ellipsoid whose volume is still positive
a half-space
the whole plane
questions.explanation: A singular \(B\) collapses the unit disk onto a lower-dimensional set, so the two-dimensional volume, which tracks \(\det B\), is zero. Positive semidefinite still makes the image an elliptical disk, only a flat one. The image of a bounded disk is bounded, so it is neither a half-space nor the whole plane.

questions.prompt: \(B = \mathrm{diag}(1,\ 2)\) and the center is the origin. One face has normal \((2,\ 0)\) and bound \(5\). The other has normal \((0,\ 1)\) and bound \(4\). What is the smaller of the two slacks, bound minus \(\lVert B a\rVert\)?
questions.explanation: The first product is \((2,\ 0)\), length \(2\), slack \(5 - 2 = 3\). The second product is \((0,\ 2)\), length \(2\), slack \(4 - 2 = 2\). The smaller slack is \(2\). Reporting \(3\) is the looser face. Reporting \(5\) or \(4\) is a bound, not a slack. Adding the slacks gives \(5\), which is not what was asked. The tighter face is the one whose slack is smaller.

questions.prompt: The containment inequality \(\lVert B a_i\rVert + a_i^T d \le b_i\) has to hold
options: for at least one inequality, since the others are then automatic
only for the inequalities that are active at the center \(d\)
only when \(B\) is a multiple of the identity
for every inequality that defines the polytope
questions.explanation: Each inequality is a half-space, and the ellipsoid has to sit in the intersection, so every half-space contributes its own inequality. One satisfied face says nothing about the opposite face. A face that misses the center can still cut the ellipsoid if \(B\) is wide. The same formula uses a general symmetric positive definite \(B\), not only a multiple of the identity.
